transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-26 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~55 min | Attendees: Tom Reed (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Alex Chen (PM, ArchiveAI), Maya Lopez (Staff ML Eng), Daniel Park (Security Architect), Sara K (Procurement)

[00:00] Tom Reed: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Tom from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with Priya our systems engineer. How are you all doing?
[00:06] Alex Chen: Good, thanks. We're excited to talk through this — trying to understand what migration would look like from our current OpenAI plus vLLM self-hosted components to Redwood Dedicated or Private.
[00:14] Priya Shah: Awesome, yeah we built an agenda around that — quick intro, your current stack and pain points, compatibility questions (vLLM/TGI), performance/eval parity, security/compliance, and then next steps.
[00:24] Maya Lopez: Sounds good. Quick context — ArchiveAI is a search and summarization product for enterprise docs. We run most generation against OpenAI gpt-4-o or 4o-mini in prod via API, but we also run a lot of local inference for high-volume batch ops using vLLM and a small TGI cluster for experimental models. Latency sensitive features (live assist) hit OpenAI, cost is material.
[00:41] Daniel Park: From security side, we need control over logs, KMS integration, SSO, and the usual SOC2/ISO checklist. Also data residency for a couple of customers.
[00:50] Tom Reed: Great, that maps nicely to what customers typically look for. Can you share rough numbers on request volume and latency targets?
[00:56] Alex Chen: Sure — in peak we see about 120 requests per second across our main endpoint, tokens per request averages 400-600, and we need p95 latency under 400ms for the live assist flows. For batch jobs, throughput and cost are the main metric. We're currently paying per-token to OpenAI and the monthly bill is, uh, material — it's in the tens of thousands but trending up.
[01:20] Priya Shah: Understood. A quick note on terminology — when you say vLLM/TGI parity, do you mean identical outputs or acceptable regression thresholds?
[01:28] Maya Lopez: Ideally parity as in output quality within our eval thresholds — we have an eval harness with BLEU-ish metrics and safety scoring. But we can tolerate small differences if latency and cost are better.
[01:36] Tom Reed: Good, that's aligned. Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools you control, predictable throughput and SLOs, plus the Private option for VPC/on-prem. We can also route to hosted models for overflow. For parity, we often run side-by-side evals and can help run benchmarks against your prompts.
[01:50] Alex Chen: Couple specific questions — does Redwood support the same model families? We use a mix: OpenAI's gpt-4o endpoints, plus some community Llama-like models via vLLM. When we onboarded, we used TGI for a few tuned weights. How compatible is the Redwood runtime?
[02:06] Priya Shah: We support a catalog of open models and we verify performance profiles; we also support loading customer models for Dedicated/Private. The serving runtime is GPU-optimized and supports attention optimizations, KV cache, quantization paths. Some differences can occur vs vLLM/TGI — sometimes tokenization or sampling default seeds create small output deltas, but we can match configurations (temp, top-p, sampling, top-k) to minimize that.
[02:30] Alex Chen: Right, tokenization differences have bitten us before.
[02:32] Maya Lopez: Also one of our big questions: for our batch jobs that run on vLLM for cost reasons, can Redwood Dedicated match that cost profile with batching/caching and quantization?
[02:42] Tom Reed: Often yes — Redwood Optimize gives recommendations on batching and quantization profiles; Dedicated lets you pick quantized variants to reduce GPU memory and increase throughput, and our autoscaler plus continuous batching can substantially drop per-token cost. We'll need to see your throughput and token distribution to give a precise TCO.
[02:57] Daniel Park: From a security perspective, how do you handle keys and logs? We need KMS/HSM integration, customer-managed keys, and audit logs with retention controls.
[03:05] Priya Shah: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and can integrate with your HSM via standard APIs; audit logs are available with configurable retention, and we provide RBAC and SSO/SAML for admin controls. For Dedicated (hosted dedicated capacity) we offer VPC peering and private networking, plus optional log forwarding to your SIEM.
[03:20] Sara K: Procurement question — what's the minimum commitment for Dedicated, and is there a path to start with Hosted then move to Dedicated without big migration cost?
[03:27] Tom Reed: Typical committed terms are monthly or annual for Reserved capacity — but you can start on Hosted and then migrate to Dedicated. We have migration tooling and an onboarding playbook — many customers start with hosted for fast validation, then commit to Dedicated when usage stabilizes.
[03:40] Alex Chen: Ok good. Another technical point: we have an existing on-prem TGI cluster for experiments. If we wanted Private on-prem, what's the lift? And will our prompts and eval harness run unchanged?
[03:51] Priya Shah: Private on-prem packages include the control plane and runtime; there is some integration work (networking, KMS, telemetry), but our packaging aims to run your eval harness without major rewrites. Tokenization differences might still cause small deltas. We provide tooling to compare logits and outputs to help you tune.
[04:09] Maya Lopez: Do you support model rollouts and canarying? We do a lot of A/B tests with model variants.
[04:15] Tom Reed: Yes — Console has rollout controls for canary deploys, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies. You can pin versions and route by policy (latency, cost, region).
[04:25] Alex Chen: Let's talk parity testing — what would you need from us to run a meaningful comparison?
[04:29] Priya Shah: Ideally your eval harness, a representative sample of prompts (say 500-2k), and current metrics (latency distribution, token counts, and safety labels). We'll run them against candidate models on Redwood-hosted and Dedicated, and provide granular diffs and regression alerts.
[04:45] Maya Lopez: We can extract that. We'll need to sanitize PII before sharing.
[04:48] Daniel Park: On compliance, if we move to Dedicated hosted in your cloud, do you provide SOC2 Type II and contractual audit support?
[04:55] Tom Reed: Redwood has SOC2 and ISO certs for our control plane; for Dedicated we provide contract language, and we can do security reviews. For Private on-prem you manage the environment and we provide the software package and evidence to assist audits. We'll send the security pack after this call.
[05:08] Sara K: How long is procurement typically for customers our size?
[05:11] Tom Reed: For mid-market with some legal negotiation, it's often 4-8 weeks once you have a draft SOW; dedicated setups can add onboarding time, typically 2-6 weeks depending on network and KMS integration.
[05:22] Alex Chen: Timeline wise we're aiming to have a pilot in Q3, ideally by mid-September. Does that seem realistic?
[05:29] Priya Shah: Yes, if we start evals now and have the parity results in 2-3 weeks, we can scope a pilot and have a Dedicated trial environment ready in parallel.
[05:38] Maya Lopez: One sticky technical detail — we use some custom tokenizer tweaks in our TGI fork. Will that break things?
[05:44] Priya Shah: Custom tokenizers are possible but will need some engineering work; for Dedicated/Private you can bring custom tokenizers, or we can help port them. There's usually a short compatibility phase.
[05:56] Alex Chen: Cost question — can you ballpark the delta vs OpenAI if we move to Dedicated for our current volume?
[06:02] Tom Reed: Roughly speaking, Dedicated is more predictable and often lower per-token for steady high volume after reserved capacity amortization. But exact math depends on batching, model size, and utilization. We'll produce a TCO comparing your current OpenAI spend vs projected Dedicated cost using your token distribution.
[06:17] [00:06:17] Unlabeled Speaker 1: (mumbled) is there downtime for model updates?
[06:21] Priya Shah: We support canarying and zero-downtime rollouts in most cases; you can route a percentage of traffic.
[06:27] Alex Chen: Any differences customers see in output vs OpenAI's gpt-4o?
[06:31] Tom Reed: Model differences are model-family specific. For open models, output tends to differ somewhat; for parity with GPT-4o you may want to run guardrails and prompt engineering. We can run red-teaming and safety evals.
[06:45] Maya Lopez: About vLLM and TGI — some of our internal infra depends on vLLM's checkpointing and prefetching behavior. How similar is Redwood's runtime?
[06:55] Priya Shah: The runtime handles KV cache and prefetch but implementation differs; we do extensive kernel selection and attention optimizations but semantics are the same. There may be subtle timing and cache flush behaviors, so we'll include checks in the parity suite.
[07:09] Alex Chen: Any limitations on model sizes for Dedicated? We run a few 70B-ish models locally.
[07:15] Tom Reed: Dedicated supports a range of model sizes; the limiting factor is GPU memory and whether you want quantized variants. For very large models we recommend multi-GPU sharding or quantized runtimes. We'll review your exact model footprints.
[07:26] Daniel Park: Network isolation — do you support VPC peering or private networking to avoid public endpoints?
[07:31] Priya Shah: Yes, VPC peering, private endpoints, and private control plane options are supported for Dedicated and Private.
[07:38] Alex Chen: Let's dive a bit into latency — our p95 requirement is 400ms. How likely is Redwood to meet that for interactive flows?
[07:46] Priya Shah: For small to mid-sized models and with prefix caching we can often meet sub-400ms p95; for very large models it's trickier. But smart batching and routing (e.g., serving the low-latency traffic from a dedicated pool) will help. We'll need your exact token length distributions to model this.
[07:59] Maya Lopez: Do you provide tracing at token level or per-request breakdowns?
[08:03] Tom Reed: Console provides per-request latency breakdowns, token-level cost, and tracing hooks. You can hook this into your observability stack.
[08:10] Alex Chen: On the operational side, if we run Dedicated, who handles OS/driver updates on the GPUs?
[08:15] Priya Shah: For Hosted Dedicated (Redwood-run), we manage the infra, drivers, and updates under the SLA. For Private on-prem, the customer typically manages the infra but we provide a supported upgrade path and automation scripts.
[08:27] [00:08:27] Alex Chen: Any gotchas with quantized models causing increased hallucinations? We've seen that historically.
[08:33] Priya Shah: Yes quantization can affect fidelity. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles by workload; for sensitive outputs we recommend fidelity checks and possibly keeping a small high-fidelity pool for those requests.
[08:45] Daniel Park: Regarding logging and PII, can you redact or avoid storing prompts?
[08:50] Tom Reed: You can configure logging policies: no-persist, redaction, or forward-only. For Private you control logs fully. For Dedicated we support redaction and log forwarding to your SIEM.
[08:59] Sara K: From contract standpoint, do you offer data residency clauses for EU customers?
[09:03] Tom Reed: Yes, we support region-based deployments and can include data residency commitments in contracts.
[09:11] Alex Chen: Ok, the rest of our timeline: we'll get procurement involved once we have a pilot cost estimate and security docs. Expect Sara and Daniel to lead that.
[09:20] Tom Reed: Perfect. Priya, do you want to summarize the technical follow-ups?
[09:24] Priya Shah: Sure — I'll run a quick compatibility check against their vLLM/TGI artifacts, run the parity evals when we get the prompt set, and surface any tokenizer or sampling diffs. We'll also prepare an infra sketch for Dedicated and Private onboarding.
[09:38] Alex Chen: We also want to validate hallucination and safety regression thresholds.
[09:41] Priya Shah: We'll include safety evals and a red-team baseline.
[09:44] [00:09:44] Alex Chen: One more procurement note — do you have pre-approved Master Services Agreement (MSA) templates for mid-market customers?
[09:51] Tom Reed: Yes we have standard MSAs; we'll share a copy.
[09:55] Maya Lopez: Regarding cutover complexity — if we start with hosted plus dedicated buffer and then migrate traffic, what happens to session state and KV caches?
[10:04] Priya Shah: We have KV cache migration tooling and prefix caching; session affinity can be maintained via routing rules. Some stateful caches will need migration but we provide scripts and best practices.
[10:15] Alex Chen: Great — let's wrap with explicit next steps.
[10:18] Tom Reed: Recap: Tom will send pricing and security pack; Priya will run parity/compat checks once you share prompts and artifacts; ArchiveAI provides prompt set and metrics; schedule follow-up infra/security deep-dive.
[10:30] Daniel Park: Sounds good. I'll gather the security questionnaire and network diagram.
[10:35] Sara K: Procurement will await the TCO.
[10:38] Tom Reed: Thanks everyone, we'll follow-up with a calendar invite for the deep-dive.
[10:44] Alex Chen: Thanks, bye.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-generated, occasional mislabels and minor transcription errors (e.g., 'K-V cash' instead of 'KV cache', 'V L LM' for vLLM).

References / links shared: Redwood Dedicated pricing (link: https://redwood.ai/pricing/dedicated), security pack note (link: https://redwood.ai/security-pack), parity eval template (internal link: https://docs.redwood/integrations/parity-eval-template)
